title: SIU not laying charges in Oakville police shooting
article: Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) says no Halton police officers will face charges in connection with the Nov. 17, 2013 fatal shooting of a distraught 22-year-old Oakville man.

In a statement issued today (July 7), SIU Director Tony Loparco said no reasonable grounds existed to charge any of five officers who opened fire on the man after he pointed what appeared to be a black handgun in their direction.
The weapon turned out to be a pellet gun.
The incident began at approximately 10 p.m. when the man sat in the driver's seat of his Kia Amanti in front of his parents' home on Oak Springs Road.
The report stated the man called his father, told him he had a gun and asked his parents to call police.
Officers soon arrived at the scene and located the man a short distance away, at the intersection of Oak Springs Road and Upper Middle Road, where he had pulled into the driveway of a residence.
Loparco said officers blocked off the area, surrounded the vehicle and tried to convince the man to surrender himself.
At 11:10 p.m., the release said, the man got out of his vehicle, holding what appeared to be a black handgun in his right hand and pointed it to his head.
He walked toward officers and stopped as several police raised their firearms and repeatedly ordered him to drop the gun. He did not listen and instead got back in his vehicle.
At about 11:45 p.m., the SIU statement indicated the man sent his mother a text message that read "Ready to go."

Shortly after, he got out of his car and walked toward police, which now included members of the Halton police Tactical Response Unit (TRU), who had subsequently arrived on the scene to join other officers.
Loparco said police continued to shout for the man to drop his weapon.
As he proceeded to point the gun in the direction of the police, five officers fired. A total of 17 shots were fired, striking the man in the upper body and head.
He was pronounced dead at the scene at 12:12 a.m. on Nov. 18.
"As it turns out, the 'gun' in the man's possession was a pellet gun. However, the officers cannot be faulted for believing it was a real handgun," said Loparco.

"They had been told the man was armed with a gun and they also observed him holding what closely resembled a 9mm handgun. In the circumstances, faced with what they reasonably believed was an imminent threat to their lives when the man pointed the 'gun' in their direction, I am satisfied the officers harboured a reasonable belief they could not otherwise protect themselves and those around them other than by a resort to lethal force."
Loparco went on to state the officers involved appear to have done everything in their power to resolve the situation peacefully, speaking with the man in attempts to convince him to surrender.
He said the officers also took measures to ensure residents in the neighbourhood and passing traffic were not placed at risk.
During the investigation into the shooting, the SIU assigned seven investigators and four forensic investigators. They interviewed eight witness officers and 17 civilian witnesses.
Five officers were designated as subject officers.
Of them, one consented to be interviewed, but did not provide his notes, and the others declined to provide a statement or a copy of their notes to the SIU, as is their legal right.

The SIU also obtained and reviewed a copy of the Halton police radio and telephone communication recordings, the subject officers' use-of-force training records and a copy of text messages the man sent to his mother.
The SIU is an arm's-length agency that investigates reports involving police where there has been death, serious injury or allegations of sexual assault.
Friends identified the man as former White Oaks Secondary School student Alex Tughan, 22.
